Hence it is written: [[John 5:18|the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he did not only break the sabbath but also said God was his Father, making himself equal to God|Quærebant Judæi eum interficere, quia non solum solvebat sabbatum, sed et patrem suum dicebat Deum, æqualem se Deo faciens]]. And when the Jews had said to him, [[John 8:25|Who art thou?|Tu quis es?]] he answered: [[John 8:25|The beginning, who also speak unto you|Principium, qui et loquor vobis]]. And Christ confirmed this same thing by miracles. For this reason he says: [[John 10:37|If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not.|Si non facio opera Patris mei, nolite credere mihi]] [[John 10:38|But if I do, though you will not believe me, believe the works|si autem facio, et si mihi non creditis, operibus credite]].

paras.t: Non in sacrificiis tuis arguam te: id est, propter omissionem sacrificiorum legalium non reprehendam te tempore novæ legis et gratiæ, quia tunc cessant; holocausta autem tua in conspectu meo sunt semper. Negatio quæ in principio versus ponitur, hic repetenda est, sicut in versu præcedentis psalmi, ubi dictum est: Non dabit Deo placationem suam, et pretium redemptionis animæ suæ, id est, nec pretium redemptionis suæ. Est igitur sensus: Sicut in sacrificiis omissis non arguam te, sic holocausta tua legalia mihi amplius accepta non sunt. Quomodo autem differant sacrificium et holocaustum, et de modo ac tempore cessationis eorum, dictum est satis prolixe in expositione psalmi tricesimi noni, cujus exordium est, Exspectans exspectavi Dominum.
paras.en: [[49:8|I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices|Non in sacrificiis tuis arguam te]]: that is, I will not rebuke thee for leaving off the legal sacrifices in the time of the new law and of grace, because they then cease; [[49:8|and thy burnt offerings are always in my sight|holocausta autem tua in conspectu meo sunt semper]]. The negative placed at the beginning of the verse is to be repeated here [so that the sense is: "nor are thy burnt offerings always in my sight"], as in a verse of the preceding psalm, where it is said: [[Ps 48:8|he shall not give to God his ransom|Non dabit Deo placationem suam]], [[Ps 48:9|Nor the price of the redemption of his soul|et pretium redemptionis animæ suæ]] [the Latin has *et pretium*, "and the price", with no negative; the Douay-Rheims already supplies it], that is, nor the price of his redemption. The sense, then, is: As I will not reprove thee for the sacrifices left off, so thy legal burnt offerings are no longer acceptable to me. How sacrifice and holocaust differ, and of the manner and time of their ceasing, has been said at sufficient length in the exposition of the thirty-ninth psalm, which begins [[Ps 39:2|With expectation I have waited for the Lord|Exspectans exspectavi Dominum]].

paras.t: Non accipiam, tempore novæ legis, de domo tua vitulos, neque de gregibus tuis hircos, ut offerantur eo modo sicut in veteri Testamento offerebantur, quamvis alio modo offerri possint ministris Ecclesiæ seu pauperibus propter Deum ad sustentaculum vitæ.
paras.en: [[49:9|I will not take|Non accipiam]], in the time of the new law, [[49:9|calves out of thy house: nor he goats out of thy flocks|de domo tua vitulos, neque de gregibus tuis hircos]], to be offered in the way they were offered in the old Testament; though they may be offered in another way, to the ministers of the Church or to the poor, for God's sake, for the support of life.

paras.t: Quoniam meæ sunt omnes feræ silvarum, id est animalia silvestria, jumenta in montibus et boves, id est animalia domestica. Omnia namque creavi.
paras.en: [[49:10|For all the beasts of the woods are mine|Quoniam meæ sunt omnes feræ silvarum]], that is, the wild animals, [[49:10|the cattle on the hills, and the oxen|jumenta in montibus et boves]], that is, the domestic animals. For I created all things.

paras.t: Cognovi omnia volatilia cæli aerii: idcirco necesse non est ut in templo meo conspectui repræsententur. Et pulchritudo agri mecum est, id est, omnis fecunditas atque ornatus terræ mihi innotescit, et in mea potestate consistit: unde nec sacrificiis, quæ de fructibus terræ fiebant, indigeo.
paras.en: [[49:11|I know all the fowls of the air|Cognovi omnia volatilia cæli]] [Denis adds *aerii*: of the heaven, that is, of the air]: therefore there is no need for them to be presented to my sight in my temple. [[49:11|and with me is the beauty of the field|Et pulchritudo agri mecum est]], that is, all the fruitfulness and adornment of the earth is known to me, and lies in my power: so that neither do I need the sacrifices that were made of the fruits of the earth.

paras.t: Si esuriero, non dicam tibi: non quod Deus in sua natura unquam esuriat; sed sensus est: Si sic mecum dispositum esset, quod cibo aut potu egerem, non necesse haberem hoc tibi insinuare, aut a te aliquid postulare; meus est enim orbis terræ et plenitudo ejus: sicut superius dictum est, Domini est terra et plenitudo ejus. Ex his autem confunditur error dicentium Deum hæc inferiora vel non creasse, vel non cognoscere particulariter et distincte, nec providentiam eorum habere.
paras.en: [[49:12|If I should be hungry, I would not tell thee|Si esuriero, non dicam tibi]]: not that God in his nature is ever hungry; but the sense is: If it were so ordered with me that I needed food or drink, I should have no need to make this known to thee, or to ask anything of thee; [[49:12|for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof|meus est enim orbis terræ et plenitudo ejus]]: as was said above, [[Ps 23:1|The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof|Domini est terra et plenitudo ejus]]. By these words is confounded the error of those who say that God either did not create these lower things, or does not know them singly and distinctly, or has no providence over them.

paras.t: Numquid manducabo, ego æternus et incommutabilis Deus, carnes taurorum, qui offeruntur, aut sanguinem hircorum immolatorum potabo, ego incorporeus Deus, in me ipso omnino perfectus ac plenus? Non utique.
paras.en: [[49:13|Shall I eat|Numquid manducabo]], I, the eternal and unchangeable God, [[49:13|the flesh of bullocks|carnes taurorum]] that are offered, [[49:13|or shall I drink the blood of goats|aut sanguinem hircorum]] that have been sacrificed, I, the incorporeal God, wholly perfect and full in myself? Surely not.

paras.t: Quum ergo sit ita, o Ecclesia catholica, Immola Deo Patri, totique Trinitati, sacrificium laudis, id est Sacramentum corporis et sanguinis Christi: quod est sacrificium per se intentum, receptum, ac ultimum, in quo beneficia Dei recoluntur, nostra peccata purgantur, et Deus summe honoratur; et redde Altissimo vota tua, id est, promissiones tuas, quas vel in Baptismo, vel in susceptione Ordinis, vel alibi promisisti, adimple: quia (ut ait Scriptura) displicet Deo infidelis et stulta promissio. Ideoque Jonas: Quæcumque (inquit) vovi, reddam pro salute Domino.
paras.en: Since this is so, then, O Catholic Church, [[49:14|Offer to God|Immola Deo]] the Father, and to the whole Trinity, [[49:14|the sacrifice of praise|sacrificium laudis]], that is, the Sacrament of the body and blood of Christ: which is the sacrifice intended for its own sake, accepted, and final, in which the benefits of God are called to mind, our sins are purged, and God is supremely honoured; [[49:14|and pay thy vows to the most High|et redde Altissimo vota tua]], that is, fulfil thy promises, which thou madest in Baptism, or in receiving Orders, or elsewhere: because (as Scripture says) [[Eccles 5:3|an unfaithful and foolish promise displeaseth him|displicet Deo infidelis et stulta promissio]]. And therefore Jonas says: [[Jon 2:10|I will pay whatsoever I have vowed for my salvation to the Lord|Quæcumque (inquit) vovi, reddam pro salute Domino]].

paras.t: Alia expositio. Denique locus iste, quoniam juxta litteralem intelligentiam planus est, moraliter exponi potest ad informationem cujuslibet nostrum, ut sit sensus: Audi, popule meus, qui a me Jesu Christo appellatus es Christianus, pro cujus redemptione me ipsum occidi permisi; et loquar tibi per inspirationem internam, per prædicatores Ecclesiæ, per studium sacræ Scripturæ. Israel, cujus conversatio est in cœlis, et revelata facie gloriam Domini contemplaris, et testificabor tibi, quod Deus tuus ego sum, qui te ab æterno elegi, teque ad fidem vocavi, ac tuæ saluti incessanter provideo. Non in sacrificiis tuis arguam te, id est, sacrificia tua interiora et exteriora mihi sunt placita, per se accepta, non figurativa. Holocausta autem tua, id est oblationes tuæ, quæ igne divini amoris totaliter inflammantur, videlicet abnegatio propriæ voluntatis, patientia in adversis, interior mortificatio spiritus, et bajulatio crucis quotidiana, oratio fervida, atque similia, in conspectu meo sunt semper, id est, mihi indesinenter placent, nec oblivioni tradentur, sed æterna beatitudine præmiabuntur. Unde et beatissimo Cornelio centurioni Angelus dixit: Orationes tuæ et eleemosynæ tuæ ascenderunt in memoriam in conspectu Dei. Et Joannes ait: Ascendit fumus incensorum de orationibus Sanctorum de manu Angeli coram Deo.
paras.en: Another exposition. Lastly, since this passage is plain according to the literal understanding, it can be expounded morally for the instruction of each of us, so that the sense is: [[49:7|Hear, O my people|Audi, popule meus]], who hast been called Christian by me, Jesus Christ, for whose redemption I allowed myself to be slain; [[49:7|and I will speak|et loquar]] to thee by inward inspiration, by the preachers of the Church, by the study of holy Scripture. [[49:7|O Israel|Israel]], whose [[Phil 3:20|conversation is in heaven|conversatio est in cœlis]], and who contemplatest [[2 Cor 3:18|the glory of the Lord with open face|revelata facie gloriam Domini]], [[49:7|and I will testify to thee|et testificabor tibi]] that [[49:7|I am God, thy God|Deus tuus ego sum]], who chose thee from eternity, and called thee to the faith, and unceasingly provide for thy salvation. [[49:8|I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices|Non in sacrificiis tuis arguam te]], that is, thy sacrifices, inward and outward, are pleasing to me, accepted for their own sake, not figurative. [[49:8|and thy burnt offerings|Holocausta autem tua]], that is, thy oblations, which are wholly set ablaze by the fire of divine love, namely the denial of one's own will, patience in adversity, the inward mortification of the spirit, and the daily carrying of the cross, fervent prayer, and the like, [[49:8|are always in my sight|in conspectu meo sunt semper]], that is, they please me unceasingly, and will not be forgotten, but will be rewarded with everlasting beatitude. Hence the Angel said to the most blessed centurion Cornelius: [[Acts 10:4|Thy prayers and thy alms are ascended for a memorial in the sight of God|Orationes tuæ et eleemosynæ tuæ ascenderunt in memoriam in conspectu Dei]]. And John says: [[Apoc 8:4|And the smoke of the incense of the prayers of the saints ascended up before God from the hand of the angel.|Ascendit fumus incensorum de orationibus Sanctorum de manu Angeli coram Deo]]

paras.t: Non accipiam de domo tua, id est de corde tuo, quod est domus cogitationum tuarum, vitulos, id est insolentes motus, seu inobedientes atque instabiles affectiones et concupiscentias, quæ instar vitulorum petulantes et inquietæ exsistunt. Hinc enim alio loco scriptum est: Væ qui dormitis in lectis eburneis, et lascivitis in stratis vestris; et, Væ qui cogitatis inutile, et operamini malum in cubilibus vestris. Neque de gregibus tuis hircos, id est, de numero operationum tuarum non recipiam, nec gratam habebo vilem illam simulationem seu hypocrisim, quæ ad modum hirci, foris severitatem seu duritiam quamdam prætendit, sed intus vanitati succumbit. Propter quod scriptum est: Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei.
paras.en: [[49:9|I will not take|Non accipiam]] [[49:9|out of thy house|de domo tua]], that is, out of thy heart, which is the house of thy thoughts, [[49:9|calves|vitulos]], that is, insolent movements, or disobedient and unstable affections and desires, which, like calves, are frisky and restless. Hence it is written in another place: [[Amos 6:1|Woe to you|Væ]] [[Amos 6:4|You that sleep upon beds of ivory, and are wanton on your couches|qui dormitis in lectis eburneis, et lascivitis in stratis vestris]]; and, [[Mich 2:1|Woe to you that devise that which is unprofitable, and work evil in your beds|Væ qui cogitatis inutile, et operamini malum in cubilibus vestris]]. [[49:9|nor he goats out of thy flocks|Neque de gregibus tuis hircos]], that is, from the number of thy works I will not receive, nor hold pleasing, that vile pretence or hypocrisy which, like the he goat, puts on outwardly a certain severity or hardness, but inwardly gives way to vanity. For this reason it is written: [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]].

paras.t: Quoniam meæ sunt omnes feræ silvarum, id est omnes animæ mundanam atque carnalem mollitiem fugientes, et duros pœnitentiæ labores viriliter sustinentes, jumenta, id est, qui jugum divini præcepti super se portant, in montibus, id est in perfectione virtutum, et boves, id est prædicatores, aliorumque cordium spirituales cultores. Cognovi, per approbationem et spiritualem inhabitationem, omnia volatilia cœli, id est eos qui terrena spernendo cœlestibus vacant, qui assumunt pennas contemplationis ut aquilæ, volant ut angeli; et pulchritudo agri, id est perfectio cordis seu exterioris conversationis, exemplaris honestas, aut probitas vitæ vulgarium, qui sunt agri prælatorum Ecclesiæ, mecum est, id est, per dissimilitudinem culpæ non distat a me, sed complacet mihi.
paras.en: [[49:10|For all the beasts of the woods are mine|Quoniam meæ sunt omnes feræ silvarum]], that is, all the souls that flee worldly and fleshly softness and manfully bear the hard labours of penance; [[49:10|the cattle|jumenta]] [*jumenta*, beasts of burden], that is, those who carry on themselves the yoke of the divine commandment, [[49:10|on the hills|in montibus]], that is, in the perfection of the virtues; [[49:10|and the oxen|et boves]], that is, preachers, the spiritual tillers of other men's hearts. [[49:11|I know|Cognovi]], by approving them and dwelling in them spiritually, [[49:11|all the fowls of the air|omnia volatilia cœli]], that is, those who, scorning earthly things, give themselves to heavenly ones, who take the wings of contemplation as eagles[[Is 40:31||]], and fly as angels; and [[49:11|the beauty of the field|pulchritudo agri]], that is, the perfection of the heart or of the outward life, an exemplary uprightness, or the goodness of life of the common people, who are the fields of the prelates of the Church, [[49:11|with me is|mecum est]]: that is, it is not set apart from me by the unlikeness of sin, but is well pleasing to me.

paras.t: Si esuriero, non dicam tibi. Esuries et desiderium, si proprie accipiantur, Deo nequaquam conveniunt, quia defectum absentiamque alicujus boni includunt. Dicitur tamen Deus esurire nostram justitiam, et desiderare nostram salutem ac perfectionem, quoniam quantum in se est, paratissimus est unicuique gratiam impertiri, nec vult mortem peccatoris, neque lætatur in perditione viventium. Unde superius dictum est: Et concupiscet rex decorem tuum. Et in Deuteronomio sic legitur: Dixit Dominus ad Moysen: Quis det talem eos, scilicet filios Israel, habere mentem, ut timeant me, et custodiant universa mandata mea, ut bene sit eis in æternum? Erit ergo sensus, Si esuriero, id est, si desideravero spiritualem profectum ac perfectionem creaturarum mearum intellectualium, non dicam tibi, id est, non indigebo a te postulare auxilium, quo desiderium meum ad effectum perducam; meus est enim orbis terræ, id est, quia tota Ecclesia per orbem diffusa, in mea potestate consistit, et plenitudo ejus, id est, universa perfectio gratiæ et virtutum cunctorum fidelium mea est, quia a me datur, conservatur et consummatur: et ita in me, per me, et ex me, potens sum perficere et salvare quemcumque voluero, neque indigeo hoc alteri indicare. Et sicut peccata hominum mihi non nocent, sic eorum salvatio mihi non prodest: propterea ratione indigentiæ meæ nullius salutem desidero, et si electorum salutem esuriero, hoc tibi reserare non egeo. Hoc est quod testatur sermo divinus: Si peccaveris, quid Deo nocebis? Porro si juste egeris, quid donabis ei? Homini qui similis est tui, nocebit impietas tua, et filium hominis adjuvabit justitia tua.
paras.en: [[49:12|If I should be hungry, I would not tell thee|Si esuriero, non dicam tibi]]. Hunger and desire, taken properly, in no way befit God, because they imply a lack and absence of some good. Yet God is said to hunger for our justice, and to desire our salvation and perfection, because for his part he is most ready to impart grace to everyone, and wills not the death of the sinner[[Ezech 18:23||]], [[Wis 1:13|neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living|neque lætatur in perditione viventium]]. Hence it was said above: [[Ps 44:12|And the king shall greatly desire thy beauty|Et concupiscet rex decorem tuum]]. And in Deuteronomy we read thus: The Lord said to Moses[[Deut 5:28||]]: [[Deut 5:29|Who shall give them|Quis det talem eos]], namely the sons of Israel, [[Deut 5:29|to have such a mind, to fear me, and to keep all my commandments|habere mentem, ut timeant me, et custodiant universa mandata mea]], [[Deut 5:29|that it may be well with them|ut bene sit eis]] [[Deut 5:29|for ever?|in æternum?]] The sense, then, will be: [[49:12|If I should be hungry|Si esuriero]], that is, if I desire the spiritual progress and perfection of my intellectual creatures, [[49:12|I would not tell thee|non dicam tibi]], that is, I shall have no need to ask help of thee to bring my desire to effect; [[49:12|for the world is mine|meus est enim orbis terræ]], that is, because the whole Church spread throughout the world lies in my power, [[49:12|and the fulness thereof|et plenitudo ejus]], that is, all the perfection of grace and of the virtues of all the faithful is mine, because it is given, kept and brought to completion by me: and so in me, through me and from me I am able to perfect and save whomsoever I will, and have no need to tell this to another. And as the sins of men do not harm me, so their salvation does not profit me: therefore I desire no one's salvation by reason of any need of mine, and if I hunger for the salvation of the elect, I need not disclose this to thee. This is what the divine word testifies: [[Job 35:6|If thou sin, what shalt thou hurt him?|Si peccaveris, quid Deo nocebis?]] [[Job 35:7|And if thou do justly, what shalt thou give him|Porro si juste egeris, quid donabis ei]]? [[Job 35:8|Thy wickedness may hurt a man that is like thee: and thy justice may help the son of man.|Homini qui similis est tui, nocebit impietas tua, et filium hominis adjuvabit justitia tua]]

paras.t: Numquid manducabo carnes taurorum? id est, numquid ego Deus, qui humiles amo, in abstinentia superborum delectationem, quæ est refectio mentis, habebo? Nequaquam. Talibus enim per Isaiam dico: Ecce in die jejunii vestri invenitur voluntas vestra. Aut sanguinem hircorum potabo? id est, numquid in apparenti mortificatione hypocritarum complacentiam possidebo? Non utique, quia in Evangelio dixi: Quum jejunatis, nolite fieri sicut hypocritæ tristes. Tu autem quum jejunas, unge caput tuum, et faciem tuam lava, ne videaris hominibus jejunans.
paras.en: [[49:13|Shall I eat the flesh of bullocks?|Numquid manducabo carnes taurorum?]] that is, shall I, God, who love the humble, take delight, which is the refreshment of the mind, in the abstinence of the proud? By no means. For to such I say through Isaias: [[Is 58:3|Behold in the day of your fast your own will is found|Ecce in die jejunii vestri invenitur voluntas vestra]]. [[49:13|or shall I drink the blood of goats?|Aut sanguinem hircorum potabo?]] that is, shall I find pleasure in the outward show of mortification of hypocrites? Surely not, for I said in the Gospel: [[Matt 6:16|when you fast, be not as the hypocrites, sad|Quum jejunatis, nolite fieri sicut hypocritæ tristes]]. [[Matt 6:17|But thou, when thou fastest anoint thy head, and wash thy face;|Tu autem quum jejunas, unge caput tuum, et faciem tuam lava]] [[Matt 6:18|That thou appear not to men to fast|ne videaris hominibus jejunans]].

paras.t: Immola Deo sacrificium laudis, id est gratiarum actionem in adversis et prosperis, omneque bonum ei adscribas, ita ut impleas quod supra inductum est, scilicet, Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus ejus in ore meo. Et redde Altissimo vota tua, id est, desideria tua coram Deo effunde, eumque dumtaxat in omni angustia deprecare: quemadmodum de viro sapiente ac justo in Ecclesiastico habetur: Cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo ad Dominum qui fecit illum, et in conspectu Altissimi deprecabitur.
paras.en: [[49:14|Offer to God the sacrifice of praise|Immola Deo sacrificium laudis]], that is, thanksgiving in adversity and in prosperity; and ascribe every good to him, so that thou fulfil what was brought in above, namely: [[Ps 33:2|I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise shall be always in my mouth.|Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus ejus in ore meo]] [[49:14|and pay thy vows to the most High|Et redde Altissimo vota tua]], that is, pour out thy desires before God, and in every distress pray to him alone: as is said in Ecclesiasticus of the wise and just man: [[Ecclus 39:6|He will give his heart to resort early to the Lord that made him, and he will pray in the sight of the most High.|Cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo ad Dominum qui fecit illum, et in conspectu Altissimi deprecabitur]]

paras.t: Peccatori autem, in peccatis perseveranti, nec voluntatem peccandi per pœnitentiam relinquenti, dixit Deus, Dei Filius incarnatus, per se ipsum et suos Prophetas: Quare tu enarras justitias meas? id est, quomodo prædicare audes verbum Dei, aliosque docere quod tu ipse non facis? et assumis testamentum meum per os tuum, id est, legem Dei sanctam et immaculatam proferre præsumis per os tuum pollutum? Hoc enim Christus per Isaiam dixit: Appropinquat populus iste ore suo, et labiis suis glorificat me, cor autem ejus longe est a me, et in vanum colunt me. Hanc ipsam quoque scripturam allegat Christus verus Deus, Pharisæos increpans, et dicens: Bene prophetavit de vobis Isaias, Populus hic labiis me honorat, etc. Unde in Ecclesiastico dicitur: Non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris.
paras.en: [[49:16|But to the sinner|Peccatori autem]], who perseveres in his sins and does not give up the will to sin by penance, [[49:16|God hath said|dixit Deus]], the incarnate Son of God, by himself and by his Prophets: [[49:16|Why dost thou declare my justices?|Quare tu enarras justitias meas?]] that is, how darest thou preach the word of God, and teach others what thou thyself doest not? [[49:16|and take my covenant in thy mouth|et assumis testamentum meum per os tuum]], that is, dost thou presume to utter the holy and spotless law of God with thy polluted mouth? For this is what Christ said through Isaias: [[Is 29:13|this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips glorify me, but their heart is far from me|Appropinquat populus iste ore suo, et labiis suis glorificat me, cor autem ejus longe est a me]], and [[Mark 7:7|in vain do they worship me|in vanum colunt me]] [these last words are not in Isaias's Latin but in the Gospel, Mark 7:7, Matt 15:9]. Christ, the true God, also cites this very scripture when rebuking the Pharisees, saying: [[Matt 15:7|well hath Isaias prophesied of you|Bene prophetavit de vobis Isaias]], [[Matt 15:8|This people honoureth me with their lips|Populus hic labiis me honorat]], etc. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 15:9|Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner|Non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris]].

paras.t: Quid ergo agendum est peccatori ad celebrandum seu prædicandum obligato? Si facit quod sibi incumbit, peccat; et si non facit, peccat, quoniam debitum negligit: sicque videtur esse perplexus. Et respondendum, quod nemo perplexus est: sic enim impossibile esset peccatum vitare. Sacerdos ergo et prædicator indignus, perplexus non est, quoniam pœnitere potest, et mutato proposito, sine peccato officium divinum exsequi. Melius tamen facit, ut communiter, quamdiu in peccato manet, non exsequendo: quia exsequendo, mortaliter peccat. Alia tamen divina, videlicet Horas canonicas, melius est persolvi quam omitti a quocumque peccatore ad Horas obligato. Nam non persolvendo, mortaliter peccat, tanquam contra præceptum Ecclesiæ agens: non autem mortaliter peccat, si eas extra gratiam exsistens persolvat, quia non est speciale præceptum de persolutione Horarum in statu salutis seu gratiæ; sicut est speciale præceptum de celebratione et administratione sacramentorum Christi ac verbi divini in statu salutis, ita ut quotiescumque sacerdos aliquod sacramentorum Christi indigne dispensat, mortaliter peccat.
paras.en: What, then, is a sinner to do who is bound to celebrate or to preach? If he does what is incumbent on him, he sins; and if he does not do it, he sins, since he neglects his duty: and so he seems to be perplexed [*perplexus*: in moral theology, one so placed that he sins whichever way he acts]. And the answer must be that no one is perplexed: for then it would be impossible to avoid sin. The unworthy priest and preacher, therefore, is not perplexed, since he can repent and, his purpose changed, carry out the divine office without sin. Yet, as a rule, so long as he remains in sin he does better by not carrying it out: because by carrying it out he sins mortally. But other divine offices, namely the canonical Hours, it is better for any sinner bound to the Hours to say than to omit. For by not saying them he sins mortally, as acting against a precept of the Church; but he does not sin mortally if he says them while he is out of grace, because there is no special precept that the Hours be said in the state of salvation or of grace; as there is a special precept about celebrating and administering the sacraments of Christ and the divine word in the state of salvation, so that whenever a priest dispenses any of the sacraments of Christ unworthily, he sins mortally.

paras.t: Tu vero, o peccator, odisti disciplinam, id est instructionem et correptionem ac debitam pœnam pro tuis excessibus, sicque de numero eorum es, de quibus scriptum est: Odio habuerunt corripientem. Quocontra Salomon monet: Disciplinam Domini, fili mi, ne abjicias, et ne deficias quum ab eo corriperis. Qui iterum ait: Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam; qui autem acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur. Et alibi: Qui abjicit disciplinam, despicit animam suam; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis. Idem autem periculum est, despicere disciplinam prælati et Dei, quoniam prælati sunt Dei vicarii. Propter quod de talibus ait Salvator: Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit. Et magnus ille prælatus sanctus Moyses dixit ad filios Israel: Non contra nos est murmur vestrum, sed contra Dominum. Si ergo salvari optamus, disciplinam Dei ac superiorum nostrorum amemus, quia scriptum est: Viro qui corripientem dura cervice contemnit, repentinus superveniet interitus. Et projecisti sermones meos retrorsum, id est, præceptis meis non paruisti, sed tuam voluntatem voluntati meæ præposuisti.
paras.en: [[49:17|Seeing thou|Tu vero]], O sinner, [[49:17|hast hated discipline|odisti disciplinam]] [*disciplina*: instruction, correction and chastisement together], that is, instruction and correction and the punishment due for thy excesses; and so thou art of the number of those of whom it is written: [[Amos 5:10|They have hated him that rebuketh|Odio habuerunt corripientem]]. Against this Solomon warns: [[Prov 3:11|My son, reject not the correction of the Lord: and do not faint when thou art chastised by him|Disciplinam Domini, fili mi, ne abjicias, et ne deficias quum ab eo corriperis]]. And again he says: [[Prov 13:18|Poverty and shame to him that refuseth instruction: but he that yieldeth to reproof shall be glorified.|Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam; qui autem acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur]] [the margin gives Prov. xiii, 13] And elsewhere: [[Prov 15:32|He that rejecteth instruction, despiseth his own soul: but he that yieldeth to reproof, possesseth understanding.|Qui abjicit disciplinam, despicit animam suam; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis]] It is the same danger to despise the discipline of a prelate and that of God, since prelates are God's vicars. For this reason the Saviour says of such: [[Luke 10:16|He that heareth you heareth me: and he that despiseth you despiseth me|Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit]]. And that great prelate, holy Moses, said to the sons of Israel: [[Ex 16:8|your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord|Non contra nos est murmur vestrum, sed contra Dominum]]. If, then, we wish to be saved, let us love the discipline of God and of our superiors, for it is written: [[Prov 29:1|The man that with a stiff neck despiseth him that reproveth him, shall suddenly be destroyed|Viro qui corripientem dura cervice contemnit, repentinus superveniet interitus]]. [[49:17|and hast cast my words behind thee|Et projecisti sermones meos retrorsum]], that is, thou hast not obeyed my precepts, but hast put thy will before mine.

paras.t: Si videbas furem, currebas cum eo, simul furando, vel furanti favendo aut cooperando, et cum adulteris portionem tuam ponebas, faciens te consocium atque participem vitiorum eorum. Est autem quoddam spirituale furtum, quo homo honorem et gloriam soli Deo debitam, sibi usurpat: et tali furto se maculat, qui superbo communicat, juxta illud, Qui communicaverit superbo, induetur superbia.
paras.en: [[49:18|If thou didst see a thief thou didst run with him|Si videbas furem, currebas cum eo]], by stealing along with him, or by favouring or helping the thief, [[49:18|and with adulterers thou hast been a partaker|et cum adulteris portionem tuam ponebas]] [literally "thou didst lay thy portion with adulterers"], making thyself the companion and sharer of their vices. Now there is a kind of spiritual theft, by which a man usurps for himself the honour and glory due to God alone: and he stains himself with such theft who has fellowship with the proud, according to the saying: [[Ecclus 13:1|he that hath fellowship with the proud, shall put on pride|Qui communicaverit superbo, induetur superbia]].

paras.t: Os tuum abundavit malitia, id est verbis illicitis, et lingua tua concinnabat dolos, id est, verba fraudulenta composuit ad alios defraudandos.
paras.en: [[49:19|Thy mouth hath abounded with evil|Os tuum abundavit malitia]], that is, with unlawful words, [[49:19|and thy tongue framed deceits|et lingua tua concinnabat dolos]], that is, it put together deceitful words to cheat others.

paras.t: Quod patet ex eo, nam Sedens in cathedra pestilentiæ, adversus fratrem, id est proximum tuum, loquebaris sermones fallaces, pungitivos, detractorios et rancorosos; et adversus filium matris tuæ, puta Ecclesiæ seu matris carnalis, ponebas scandalum, præbendo ei occasionem ruinæ, seu offendiculum verbo vel facto inordinato: quod est contra admonitionem Apostoli, ubi ait: Non ergo amplius invicem judicemus; sed hoc judicate magis, ne ponatis offendiculum fratri vel scandalum. Noli illum perdere, pro quo Christus mortuus est. Salvator quoque: Væ (inquit) homini illi, per quem scandalum venit. Est nihilo minus scandalum quoddam Pharisæorum, quod venit ex malitia et cæcitate scandalizati, non ex defectu scandalizantis: et tale non est semper vitandum. Nam, ut Evangelista testatur, quum discipuli Christo dixissent, Scis quia Pharisæi, audito hoc verbo, scandalizati sunt? ipse respondit: Sinite illos, cæci sunt et duces cæcorum. Scandalum autem pusillorum vitandum est: imo interdum quædam non mala, vel etiam bona non jussa, omittenda sunt, differenda, aut abscondenda, ne scandalizentur pusilli, sicut dicit Apostolus: Si esca scandalizat fratrem meum, non manducabo carnes in æternum. Qui autem scandalizatur, pusillus est: perfecti enim non scandalizantur, secundum Hieronymum; nec scandalizant, secundum Thomam. Vehementer ergo studendum est nobis, ut simus ad invicem exemplares.
paras.en: This is plain from the following, for [[49:20|Sitting|Sedens]] in the chair of pestilence [Denis adds these words from Ps 1:1], [[49:20|thou didst speak|loquebaris]] [[49:20|against thy brother|adversus fratrem]], that is, thy neighbour, words that were false, stinging, slanderous and spiteful; and [[49:20|against thy mother's son|adversus filium matris tuæ]], that is, of the Church or of thy mother in the flesh, [[49:20|didst lay a scandal|ponebas scandalum]] [scandal: a word or deed that gives another occasion of spiritual ruin], giving him occasion of a fall, or a stumbling block, by a disordered word or deed: which is against the admonition of the Apostle, where he says: [[Rom 14:13|Let us not therefore judge one another any more. But judge this rather, that you put not a stumblingblock or a scandal|Non ergo amplius invicem judicemus; sed hoc judicate magis, ne ponatis offendiculum fratri vel scandalum]]. [[Rom 14:15|Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died|Noli illum perdere, pro quo Christus mortuus est]]. The Saviour too: [[Matt 18:7|woe|Væ]], he says, [[Matt 18:7|to that man by whom the scandal cometh|homini illi, per quem scandalum venit]]. There is nonetheless a certain scandal of the Pharisees, which comes from the malice and blindness of the one scandalized, not from a fault in the one who scandalizes: and such scandal is not always to be avoided. For, as the Evangelist testifies, when the disciples had said to Christ, [[Matt 15:12|Dost thou know that the Pharisees, when they heard this word, were scandalized?|Scis quia Pharisæi, audito hoc verbo, scandalizati sunt?]] he answered: [[Matt 15:14|Let them alone: they are blind, and leaders of the blind|Sinite illos, cæci sunt et duces cæcorum]]. But the scandal of the little ones is to be avoided: indeed sometimes certain things that are not evil, or even good things not commanded, are to be left undone, put off or hidden, lest the little ones be scandalized, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 8:13|if meat scandalize my brother, I will never eat flesh|Si esca scandalizat fratrem meum, non manducabo carnes in æternum]]. Now whoever is scandalized is little: for the perfect are not scandalized, according to Jerome; nor do they scandalize, according to Thomas. We must therefore strive earnestly to be examples to one another.

paras.t: Hæc mala fecisti, o peccator, et tacui. Christus enim frequenter diu exspectat, nec statim se vindicat. Existimasti inique, quod ero tui similis? id est, an propter meam longanimem exspectationem arbitraris quod peccata tua dissimulabo, aut eis favebo, nec tibi pœnas justas infligam, quemadmodum justis gloriam tribuam? Arguam te, vel ante mortem, vel in morte, et maxime in die generalis judicii, et statuam contra faciem tuam, id est, peccata tua tibi manifeste objiciam, et de omnibus operibus tuis rationem requiram, tam in hora mortis, quam in die novissimo.
paras.en: [[49:21|These things hast thou done|Hæc mala fecisti]] [Denis reads *Hæc mala*, "these evil things"], O sinner, [[49:21|and I was silent|et tacui]]. For Christ often waits long, and does not avenge himself at once. [[49:21|Thou thoughtest unjustly that I should be like to thee|Existimasti inique, quod ero tui similis]]? that is, dost thou suppose, because of my long-suffering patience, that I will overlook thy sins or favour them, and not inflict just punishment on thee, as I shall grant glory to the just? [[49:21|I will reprove thee|Arguam te]], either before death, or at death, and above all on the day of the general judgment, [[49:21|and set before thy face|et statuam contra faciem tuam]], that is, I will set thy sins openly before thee, and demand an account of all thy works, both in the hour of death and on the last day.

paras.t: Intelligite hæc, id est, intime ea pensate, qui obliviscimini Deum, non curantes ejus præcepta, nec pensantes ejus horrenda judicia, nec attendentes ejus gloriosa promissa; nequando rapiat, id est, ne Deus aliquo tempore vos imparatos ab hac vita abstrahat, et suo tribunali præsentari præcipiat, et non sit qui eripiat vos de justo ejus judicio: quia in mortali peccato morientem nemo redimere potest, nisi ex speciali gratia reducatur ad pristinum statum.
paras.en: [[49:22|Understand these things|Intelligite hæc]], that is, weigh them inwardly, [[49:22|you that forget God|qui obliviscimini Deum]], not caring for his precepts, nor weighing his dreadful judgments, nor heeding his glorious promises; [[49:22|lest he snatch you away|nequando rapiat]], that is, lest God at some time take you unprepared out of this life, and order you to be brought before his tribunal, [[49:22|and there be none to deliver you|et non sit qui eripiat]] from his just judgment: because no one can redeem one who dies in mortal sin, unless by a special grace he be brought back to his former state.

paras.t: Sacrificium laudis: de quo jam dictum est, Immola Deo sacrificium laudis; honorificabit me, quia per se acceptum est; et illic iter, id est, in tali sacrificio, scilicet in laude Deo reverenter oblata, est via, quo ostendam illi, tale sacrificium immolanti, salutare Dei, id est Christum humani generis salvatorem. Nam per sacrificium laudis ad Christi visionem in præsenti per fidem, et in futuro per speciem, pervenitur: imo laudatio Dei, est optima via beatitudinem acquirendi, secundum quod Dominus alio loco asserit: Quicumque glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum.
paras.en: [[49:23|The sacrifice of praise|Sacrificium laudis]], of which it has already been said, [[49:14|Offer to God the sacrifice of praise|Immola Deo sacrificium laudis]], [[49:23|shall glorify me|honorificabit me]], because it is accepted for its own sake; [[49:23|and there is the way|et illic iter]], that is, in such a sacrifice, namely in praise reverently offered to God, there is the way [[49:23|by which I will shew him|quo ostendam illi]], him who offers such a sacrifice, [[49:23|the salvation of God|salutare Dei]] [*salutare*, "salvation", which Denis takes of the Saviour], that is, Christ the saviour of the human race. For by the sacrifice of praise one comes to the vision of Christ, in this life by faith, and in the life to come by sight: indeed the praise of God is the best way of gaining beatitude, as the Lord declares in another place: [[1 Kings 2:30|whosoever shall glorify me, him will I glorify|Quicumque glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum]].

paras.t: Ecce quam admiranda est virtus hujus psalmi, quam fructuosa est ejus scientia. Et quis laudem ejus exprimere queat? in quo benignitas primi adventus Domini Salvatoris tam pulchre describitur, eo quod Deus deorum per se ipsum locutus sit mundo, universos ad suam fidem invitans; in quo insuper terror futuri judicii seu secundi adventus ejusdem tam terribiliter explicatur, multaque alia præclarissime decantantur. Conemur ergo humilitatem, paupertatem, ac pietatem primi adventus Christi ita sectari, ut in secundo ejus adventu, majestatem et gloriam atque justitiam ejus sine formidine mereamur conspicere. Proponamus oculo mentis nostræ, et in corde nostro fortiter depingamus qualitatem futuri judicii: quam horrendum erit videre elementa ardentia, acies angelorum, facies dæmonum, monstruosissima corpora reproborum, scissa alta cœlorum, terram hiantem, Judicem irascentem, et exspectare inevitabilem æternæ damnationis sententiam, videreque ante se parata sempiterna supplicia. Si ista atque similia modo sollicite consideramus, tunc procul dubio in die tanti horroris securi gaudentesque stabimus.
paras.en: See how wonderful is the power of this psalm, how fruitful the knowledge of it. And who could express its praise? In it the kindness of the first coming of the Lord Saviour is so beautifully described, in that [[49:1|The God of gods|Deus deorum]] spoke to the world by himself, inviting all to his faith; in it, moreover, the terror of the judgment to come, that is, of his second coming, is set forth so terribly, and many other things are most nobly sung. Let us strive, then, so to follow the humility, poverty and lovingkindness of Christ's first coming, that at his second coming we may deserve to behold his majesty and glory and justice without dread. Let us set before the eye of our mind, and paint firmly in our heart, what the judgment to come will be like: how dreadful it will be to see the elements burning, the ranks of the angels, the faces of the demons, the most monstrous bodies of the reprobate, the heights of the heavens rent, the earth gaping, the Judge angry; and to await the inevitable sentence of eternal damnation, and to see everlasting torments made ready before one. If we consider these and like things carefully now, then without doubt we shall stand secure and rejoicing in the day of so great a horror.

paras.t: Precatio. Dirige, Domine, super nos oculos misericordiæ, et in die tribulationis, potentiæ tuæ brachio nos erue: ut et te honorificemus, ac pro nostra liberatione sacrificium tibi laudis devote immolemus.
paras.en: Prayer. Direct, O Lord, the eyes of thy mercy upon us, and [[49:15|in the day of trouble|in die tribulationis]] deliver us by the arm of thy power: that we may both glorify thee, and for our deliverance devoutly offer thee the sacrifice of praise.

50.title: EXPOSITIO PSALMI QUINQUAGESIMI : MISERERE MEI, DEUS, SECUNDUM, ETC.
50.title_en: Exposition of the fiftieth psalm: Have mercy on me, O God, according to, etc.

paras.t: Declarandi jam psalmi iste est titulus : Psalmus David, quum venit ad eum Nathan propheta, quando intravit ad Bethsabee. Hic autem titulus planus est scientibus historiam secundi libri Regum : in qua narratur quemadmodum David cum uxore Uriæ adulterium fecit; et postea, scilicet post mortem Uriæ, quando David duxit eam in conjugem, tunc Nathan venit ad David, et eum de tanto piaculo arguit. Advertensque David crimen commissum, vehementissime doluit, atque ex cordiali pœnitentia hunc psalmum conscripsit : in quo (in persona propria, seu cujuslibet intime pœnitentis) affectuosissime loquitur, humillime orat, ardentissima verba effundit. Tanta enim est virtus et dignitas psalmi istius, ut ab ejus præconio lingua deficiat.
paras.en: The title of the psalm now to be explained is this: [[50:1|a psalm of David|Psalmus David]], [[50:2|When Nathan the prophet came to him|quum venit ad eum Nathan propheta]], [[50:2|after he had sinned with Bethsabee|quando intravit ad Bethsabee]] [the Latin says literally "when he went in to Bethsabee"]. This title is plain to those who know the history in the second book of Kings, where it is told how David committed adultery with the wife of Urias[[2 Kings 11:1||]]; and how afterwards, that is, after the death of Urias, when David had taken her to wife, Nathan came to David and rebuked him for so great a sin[[2 Kings 12:1||]]. And David, seeing the crime he had committed, grieved most vehemently, and out of heartfelt penitence wrote this psalm, in which (in his own person, or in that of any soul deeply penitent) he speaks most tenderly, prays most humbly, and pours out most ardent words. For so great is the power and dignity of this psalm that the tongue fails in its praise.

paras.t: Ait ergo : Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam. O verbum salubre, o consilium unicum, o singulare refugium ! Quum ignoret peccator quid agere, quid incipere, quo se vertere debeat, hoc unicum ei manet solatium, tutum refugium, prudentissimumque consilium, ut dicat : Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam. Quum propriorum scelerum mole opprimitur, quum ingratitudinis suæ excessu terretur, dum peccatorum suorum multitudine ac magnitudine contabescit, hoc solum restat, ut dicat : Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam. Ideo enim scriptum est : Quum ignoremus quid agere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te.
paras.en: He says, then: [[50:3|Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy|Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam]]. O wholesome word, O counsel without peer, O singular refuge! When the sinner knows not what to do, what to begin, where to turn, this one comfort remains to him, this safe refuge and most prudent counsel: to say, [[50:3|Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy|Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam]]. When he is crushed by the weight of his own crimes, when he is terrified by the excess of his ingratitude, while he wastes away at the number and greatness of his sins, this alone remains: to say, [[50:3|Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy|Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam]]. For this is why it is written: [[2 Par 20:12|as we know not what to do, we can only turn our eyes to thee|Quum ignoremus quid agere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te]].

paras.t: Denique duo præcipue pensanda sunt pœnitenti, imo cuilibet viatori oranti, videlicet propria miseria et divina misericordia : quatenus ex consideratione suæ miseriæ ad orationem festinet, se ipsum humiliet et accuset ; ex consideratione autem misericordiæ Dei respiret, spem veniæ sumat, Deumque cum incessabili fiducia invocet. Si enim peccator vitiorum suorum enormitatem perpendens, divinam justitiam solummodo penset, desperare poterit potius quam orare : quemadmodum accidit Cain, qui dixit, Major est iniquitas mea quam ut veniam merear ; ac Judæ proditori, qui quum dixisset, Peccavi tradens sanguinem innocentem, abiens, laqueo se suspendit, et crepuit medius. Nihilo minus considerare debet peccator divinam justitiam, ut sciat se puniendum, ac timeat ; divinam quoque potentiam, ut sciat se non posse evadere aut resistere ; atque divinam sapientiam, ut sciat se non posse latere. Sed quoniam horum consideratione aliud nihil incutit reæ conscientiæ, nisi horrorem ac mœrorem, restat ut ad solam Dei misericordiam se convertat, et ex ejus contemplatione consolationem fiduciamque concipiat. Unde beatus Job considerans omnipotentiam, sapientiam atque justitiam Judicis sui, ad solam misericordiam se transferens, ait : Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo ; et si voluerit cum eo contendere, non poterit respondere unum pro mille. Etiam si habuero quidpiam justum, non respondebo ei, sed ut meum judicem deprecabor. Et si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me. Etiam si simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea.
paras.en: Further, two things above all are to be weighed by the penitent, nay by every wayfarer who prays [that is, every man still in this life, on the way to his heavenly home]: namely his own misery and the divine mercy; so that from the consideration of his misery he may hasten to prayer and humble and accuse himself, and from the consideration of God's mercy he may breathe again, take hope of pardon, and call upon God with unceasing confidence. For if the sinner, weighing the enormity of his vices, should consider the divine justice only, he might despair rather than pray: as happened to Cain, who said, [[Gen 4:13|My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon|Major est iniquitas mea quam ut veniam merear]]; and to Judas the traitor, who, when he had said, [[Matt 27:4|I have sinned in betraying innocent blood|Peccavi tradens sanguinem innocentem]], [[Matt 27:5|went and hanged himself with an halter|abiens, laqueo se suspendit]], and [[Acts 1:18|burst asunder in the midst|crepuit medius]]. None the less the sinner ought to consider the divine justice, so as to know that he deserves punishment, and to fear; and the divine power, so as to know that he cannot escape or resist; and the divine wisdom, so as to know that he cannot lie hidden. But since the consideration of these strikes nothing into a guilty conscience but horror and grief, it remains for him to turn to the mercy of God alone, and from the contemplation of it to conceive comfort and confidence. Hence blessed Job, considering the omnipotence, wisdom and justice of his Judge, and betaking himself to mercy alone, says: [[Job 9:2|man cannot be justified, compared with God|Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo]]; and [[Job 9:3|If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one for a thousand|si voluerit cum eo contendere, non poterit respondere unum pro mille]]. [[Job 9:15|I, who although I should have any just thing, would not answer, but would make supplication to my judge|Etiam si habuero quidpiam justum, non respondebo ei, sed ut meum judicem deprecabor]]. And [[Job 9:20|If I would justify myself, my own mouth shall condemn me|si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me]]. [[Job 9:21|Although I should be simple, even this my soul shall be ignorant of|Etiam si simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea]].

paras.t: Peccator itaque in conspectu summi Judicis omnia inspicientis, se ipsum constituens, et peccatorum suorum enormitatem exhorrens, perpendensque quoque se divinæ justitiæ rigorem tolerare non posse, nec divinæ sapientiæ oculum aliquid posse latere, neque divinæ potentiæ se posse resistere, ad solam misericordissimi Creatoris pietatem confugiens, dicat : Miserere mei, Deus : id est, quoniam ego miser, tuque misericors, ideo miserere mei, compatiendo, non indignando ; ignoscendo, non ulciscendo ; succurrendo, non relinquendo. Noli in me ostendere virtutem tuæ justitiæ, ne sim vas contumeliæ seu iræ in interitum, sed abyssum tuæ clementiæ, ut sim vas misericordiæ in salutem. Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo, neque secundum peccata mea restituas mihi ; sed quoniam ego multum miser sum (peccata enim miserum faciunt peccatorem), et tu multum misericors, ideo, Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam : quæ quum sit immensa, omnem miseriam meam in infinitum excedit. Sicut igitur magnitudo maris guttam aquæ quasi nihil absorbet ; sic misericordiæ tuæ immensitas, o Domine, omnem miseriam meam consumat et æternaliter deleat.
paras.en: The sinner, then, setting himself in the sight of the supreme Judge who beholds all things, shuddering at the enormity of his sins, and weighing also that he cannot bear the rigour of the divine justice, that nothing can lie hidden from the eye of the divine wisdom, and that he cannot resist the divine power, should flee to the loving-kindness of the most merciful Creator alone, and say: [[50:3|Have mercy on me, O God|Miserere mei, Deus]]: that is, since I am wretched and thou art merciful [the play on *miser*, "wretched", and *misericors*, "merciful", is lost in English], therefore have mercy on me, by pitying, not by being angry; by forgiving, not by avenging; by helping, not by forsaking. Do not shew in me the might of thy justice, lest I be a vessel of dishonour, or of wrath unto destruction[[Rom 9:21||]] [the words "of wrath unto destruction" are from Rom 9:22], but the abyss of thy clemency, that I may be a vessel of mercy unto salvation[[Rom 9:23||]]. [[Ps 142:2|enter not into judgment with thy servant|Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo]], nor repay me according to my sins[[Ps 102:10||]]; but since I am very wretched (for sins make the sinner wretched), and thou art very merciful, therefore [[50:3|Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy|Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam]]: which, being boundless, infinitely exceeds all my misery. As, then, the greatness of the sea swallows up a drop of water as though it were nothing, so may the immensity of thy mercy, O Lord, consume all my misery and blot it out for ever.

paras.t: Et secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum, dele iniquitatem meam. Deus naturaliter misericors est, et proprium est sibi, misereri ac parcere. Propter quod scriptum est, Quia solus pius est. Miseratio autem Dei active significata, est ipsa misericordia Dei, secundum quod actualiter miseretur. Et quamvis misericordia Dei et miseratio ejus in ipso Deo sit una ac simplex, dicuntur tamen misericordiæ Dei multæ, et miserationes ejus quamplurimæ, propter diversitatem seu multitudinem suorum effectuum. Miseratio vero Dei passive accepta, est misericordiæ suæ effectus. Est igitur sensus : Secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum, id est, secundum quod tu multis modis variisque auxiliis misereri potes : secundum hoc, dele iniquitatem meam, quoniam infinitis modis et indeficientibus auxiliis succurrere vales : et hanc, precor, multitudinem miserationum tuarum ostende in me. Vel sic : Secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum, id est, secundum quod prioribus sanctis et peccatoribus conversis multipliciter misertus es : secundum hoc, postulo ut mihi misericordiam multiformem impendas, et iniquitatem omissionis et commissionis ab anima mea deleas. Non oro, o Domine, ut secundum multitudinem meritorum meorum mecum agas, sed secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum iniquitatem meam amoveas. Et hoc est quod Daniel postulat : Per temetipsum inclina, Deus meus, aurem tuam. Neque enim in justificationibus nostris prosternimus preces ante faciem tuam, sed in miserationibus tuis multis. Exaudi, Domine ; placare, Domine ; ne moreris. Porro nunquam mortale peccatum deletur, nisi gratia infundatur. Per hoc ergo quod orat iniquitatem suam deleri, implicite postulat gratiam sibi infundi.
paras.en: [[50:3|And according to the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my iniquity|Et secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum, dele iniquitatem meam]]. God is merciful by nature, and it is proper to him to have mercy and to spare. Hence it is written, [[Apoc 15:4|For thou only art holy|Quia solus pius est]] [Denis has *pius est*, "he only is loving", for *pius es*; *pius* means loving and merciful, which the Douay-Rheims renders "holy"]. Now God's tender mercy [*miseratio*], taken in the active sense, is God's mercy itself, according as he actually shews mercy. And although God's mercy and his tender mercy are in God himself one and simple, yet God's mercies are said to be many, and his tender mercies very many, because of the diversity or multitude of their effects. God's tender mercy taken in the passive sense is the effect of his mercy. The sense, then, is: [[50:3|according to the multitude of thy tender mercies|Secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum]], that is, according as thou canst shew mercy in many ways and with various helps: according to this, [[50:3|blot out my iniquity|dele iniquitatem meam]], since thou art able to succour in infinite ways and with unfailing helps; and shew forth in me, I pray, this multitude of thy tender mercies. Or thus: [[50:3|according to the multitude of thy tender mercies|Secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum]], that is, according as thou hast had mercy in manifold ways on the saints before me and on sinners who were converted: according to this, I ask that thou bestow on me a manifold mercy, and blot out from my soul the iniquity of omission and of commission. I do not pray, O Lord, that thou deal with me according to the multitude of my merits, but that thou take away my iniquity according to the multitude of thy tender mercies. And this is what Daniel asks: [[Dan 9:19|for thy own sake|Per temetipsum]] [[Dan 9:18|Incline, O my God, thy ear|inclina, Deus meus, aurem tuam]]. [[Dan 9:18|for it is not for our justifications that we present our prayers before thy face, but for the multitude of thy tender mercies|Neque enim in justificationibus nostris prosternimus preces ante faciem tuam, sed in miserationibus tuis multis]]. [[Dan 9:19|O Lord, hear: O Lord, be appeased|Exaudi, Domine ; placare, Domine]]: [[Dan 9:19|delay not|ne moreris]]. Moreover, a mortal sin is never blotted out unless grace is poured in. By asking, then, that his iniquity be blotted out, he implicitly asks that grace be poured into him.

paras.t: Amplius lava me ab iniquitate mea, id est, per infusionem gratiæ tuæ purga animam meam a macula quam peccando incurri, et præsta mihi compunctionem internam ac fontem lacrimarum, quibus ab immunditiis vitiorum laver, quemadmodum præcipitur mihi : Lava a malitia cor tuum. Et a peccato meo munda me, dimittendo pœnam et culpam, ornandoque mentem claritate gratiarum et virtutum. Peccata namque animam meam deturpant ac maculant, atque diabolo similem faciunt, et sanctæ Trinitati difformem, omneque bonum gratiæ tuæ ab ea impediunt : sicut Jeremias propheta ait, Peccata vestra prohibuerunt bonum a vobis : et Isaias, Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter Deum vestrum et vos, et peccata vestra absconderunt faciem ejus a vobis. Unde in libro Job legitur : Numquid grande est ut consoleatur te Deus ? Sed verba tua prava hoc prohibent. Quoniam ergo, o Domine, Isaia teste, hic est omnis fructus, ut auferatur peccatum ; oro, lava me ab iniquitate mea, quatenus impleatur in me quod scriptum est de te : Non immittet Dominus ultra furorem suum, quoniam volens misericordiam est ; revertetur, et miserebitur nostri. Deponet omnes iniquitates nostras, et projiciet in profundum maris omnia peccata nostra. Imple quoque in me quod quærentibus te per Isaiam promisisti : Si fuerint peccata vestra ut coccinum, quasi nix dealbabuntur ; et si fuerint rubra quasi vermiculus, velut lana alba erunt.
paras.en: [[50:4|Wash me yet more from my iniquity|Amplius lava me ab iniquitate mea]], that is, by the pouring in of thy grace cleanse my soul from the stain I incurred by sinning, and grant me inward compunction and a fountain of tears, by which I may be washed from the uncleanness of vices, as I am commanded: [[Jer 4:14|Wash thy heart from wickedness|Lava a malitia cor tuum]]. [[50:4|and cleanse me from my sin|Et a peccato meo munda me]], by remitting the punishment and the guilt, and adorning my mind with the brightness of graces and virtues. For sins disfigure and stain my soul, make it like the devil and unlike the Holy Trinity, and keep from it every good of thy grace: as Jeremias the prophet says, [[Jer 5:25|your sins have withholden good things from you|Peccata vestra prohibuerunt bonum a vobis]]; and Isaias, [[Is 59:2|your iniquities have divided between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you|Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter Deum vestrum et vos, et peccata vestra absconderunt faciem ejus a vobis]]. Hence we read in the book of Job: [[Job 15:11|Is it a great matter that God should comfort thee? but thy wicked words hinder this|Numquid grande est ut consoleatur te Deus ? Sed verba tua prava hoc prohibent]]. Since then, O Lord, on the witness of Isaias, [[Is 27:9|this is all the fruit, that the sin thereof should be taken away|hic est omnis fructus, ut auferatur peccatum]], I pray: [[50:4|Wash me yet more from my iniquity|lava me ab iniquitate mea]], so that there may be fulfilled in me what is written of thee: [[Mich 7:18|he will send his fury in no more, because he delighteth in mercy|Non immittet Dominus ultra furorem suum, quoniam volens misericordiam est]]; [[Mich 7:19|He will turn again, and have mercy on us: he will put away our iniquities: and he will cast all our sins into the bottom of the sea|revertetur, et miserebitur nostri. Deponet omnes iniquitates nostras, et projiciet in profundum maris omnia peccata nostra]]. Fulfil in me also what thou didst promise through Isaias to those who seek thee: [[Is 1:18|if your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made as white as snow: and if they be red as crimson, they shall be white as wool|Si fuerint peccata vestra ut coccinum, quasi nix dealbabuntur ; et si fuerint rubra quasi vermiculus, velut lana alba erunt]].

paras.t: Ideo autem peto a peccato mundari, Quoniam iniquitatem meam ego cognosco. Non illam abscondo, nec me ipsum excuso, nec dæmoni, nec alteri illam imputo, sed peccatum meum confiteor. Quoniam ergo initium bonorum, est confessio malorum seu recognitio peccatorum, ignosce mihi, et spiritualem vitam in me ordina ac renova. Tu ergo, si misericordiam consequi cupis, peccatum tuum agnosce, nec in oculo fratris tui festucam inspicias, sed trabem quæ in oculo tuo est adspice, dicque quod scriptum est : Peccavi, et vere deliqui, et ut eram dignus, non recepi. Hinc apud Jeremiam Dominus ait excusanti se ipsum : Ego judicio contendam tecum, eo quod dixeris, Non peccavi. Si autem vis scire quid sit vere iniquitatem propriam recognoscere, audi Manassen orantem, et dicentem : Peccavi, Domine, peccavi, et iniquitatem meam agnosco. Peto rogans te, ne simul perdas me cum iniquitatibus meis. Et peccatum meum contra me est semper, id est, semper displicet mihi, et detestor illud. Alia littera habet, Coram me est semper, et redit in idem. Nam sensus est : Semper objicio illud considerationi meæ, et inspicio illud, quatenus ipsum deplangam.
paras.en: And I ask to be cleansed from sin for this reason: [[50:5|For I know my iniquity|Quoniam iniquitatem meam ego cognosco]]. I do not hide it, nor excuse myself, nor lay it to the devil or to anyone else, but I confess my sin. Since, then, the beginning of good things is the confession of evil things, or the acknowledging of sins, forgive me, and set in order and renew the spiritual life in me. Thou, then, if thou desirest to obtain mercy, acknowledge thy sin; do not look at the mote in thy brother's eye, but behold the beam that is in thy own eye[[Matt 7:4||]][[Matt 7:5||]] [the margin gives Matt. vii, 4, 5; Denis's wording is closest to Matt 7:3]; and say what is written: [[Job 33:27|I have sinned, and indeed I have offended, and I have not received what I have deserved|Peccavi, et vere deliqui, et ut eram dignus, non recepi]]. Hence in Jeremias the Lord says to one who excuses himself: [[Jer 2:35|I will contend with thee in judgment, because thou hast said: I have not sinned|Ego judicio contendam tecum, eo quod dixeris, Non peccavi]]. But if thou wilt know what it is truly to acknowledge one's own iniquity, hear Manasses praying and saying: I have sinned, O Lord, I have sinned, and I acknowledge my iniquity. I ask, beseeching thee, that thou destroy me not together with my iniquities [from the Prayer of Manasses, which stands in the appendix of the Vulgate, outside the canon]. [[50:5|and my sin is always before me|Et peccatum meum contra me est semper]], that is, it always displeases me, and I detest it. Another text has "is always before me" [*coram me*, where the Vulgate has *contra me*, literally "against me"], and it comes to the same thing. For the sense is: I always set it before my consideration and look upon it, so as to bewail it.

paras.t: Tibi soli peccavi : quia omne peccatum est contra legem tuam aliquo modo ; nec peccatum in proximum vel se ipsum habet rationem peccati, nisi in quantum originaliter contrariatur aut dissonat ordini tuæ sapientiæ atque justitiæ, quoniam tu es mensura, causa, et fons universæ sanctitatis. Et malum coram te feci, id est, te præsente, et omnia inspiciente, non sum veritus facere malum : et in hoc aggravatur iniquitas mea, quoniam tuam præsentiam tam parum curavi. Ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis, et vincas quum judicaris. Secundum expositores communiter, subintelligitur aliquid hoc loco, videlicet, Remitte mihi, seu Miserere mihi. Ut sit sensus : Tibi soli peccavi, et malum coram te feci, et peto ut mihi remittas ac miserearis, ut justificeris, id est, justus ac verax inveniaris, in sermonibus tuis, quibus per os sanctorum Prophetarum pœnitentibus veniam promisisti, sicut est illud : Sanabo contritiones eorum, diligam eos spontanee, quia aversus est furor meus ab eis. Et vincas, id est, in justitia ceteros excedas ac superes, quum judicaris, id est, dum aliis judicium tuum innotescit, ac per hoc judicant te bene et recte fecisse, sicque judicium tuum justificant.
paras.en: [[50:6|To thee only have I sinned|Tibi soli peccavi]]: because every sin is in some way against thy law; nor has a sin against one's neighbour or against oneself the nature of sin except in so far as at root it is contrary to, or out of tune with, the order of thy wisdom and justice, since thou art the measure, cause and fountain of all holiness. [[50:6|and have done evil before thee|Et malum coram te feci]], that is, with thee present and beholding all things, I did not fear to do evil: and in this my iniquity is made heavier, that I cared so little for thy presence. [[50:6|that thou mayst be justified in thy words, and mayst overcome when thou art judged|Ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis, et vincas quum judicaris]]. According to the expositors generally, something is to be understood here, namely, Forgive me, or, Have mercy on me; so that the sense is: To thee only have I sinned, and have done evil before thee, and I ask that thou forgive me and have mercy on me, [[50:6|that thou mayst be justified|ut justificeris]], that is, be found just and truthful, [[50:6|in thy words|in sermonibus tuis]], in which, through the mouth of the holy Prophets, thou hast promised pardon to penitents; as in this saying: [[Osee 14:5|I will heal their breaches, I will love them freely: for my wrath is turned away from them|Sanabo contritiones eorum, diligam eos spontanee, quia aversus est furor meus ab eis]]. [[50:6|and mayst overcome|Et vincas]], that is, mayst exceed and surpass others in justice, [[50:6|when thou art judged|quum judicaris]], that is, when thy judgment becomes known to others, and so they judge that thou hast done well and rightly, and thus justify thy judgment.

paras.t: Sed melius arbitror ut nihil subintelligatur : imo si bene pensemus, nihil subintelligendum videbitur. Debemus enim sequi expositionem Apostoli. Apostolus vero introducit atque allegat ad Romanos hæc verba hoc modo : Est autem Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax, sicut scriptum est, Ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis, et vincas quum judicaris. Patet ergo, quod secundum intentionem Apostoli, sanctus David ad hunc sensum prædicta verba induxit, quod Deus ex nostra iniquitate justificatur, et vincit quum judicatur. Et hoc ex sequentibus verbis Apostoli clarius liquet : subdit enim, Si autem iniquitas nostra justitiam Dei commendat, quid dicemus ? Sciendum tamen, quod Deum ex nostro peccato justificari, et glorificari, et vincere quum judicatur, intelligi potest dupliciter. Primo, causaliter et directe : et ita verum non est. Secundo, occasionaliter et indirecte seu consecutive : et ita verum est, sicut inducit Apostolus. Et iste est sensus litteralior, quamvis prima expositio stare possit. Est itaque sensus : Tibi soli peccavi et malum coram te feci, ut ex hoc occasionaliter et consecutive justificeris in sermonibus tuis, quibus dixisti per Prophetas, nullum hominem esse sine peccato, sed omnem hominem esse mendacem verbo aut opere, seu aliquo vitio : quia ut in libro Job scriptum est, Nemo mundus a sorde. Vel, In sermonibus tuis, quibus peccatorem damnas et punis, justum vero salvas atque glorificas. Malum namque meum a te bene ordinatum, id est juste punitum seu pie indultum, cedit ad gloriam tuam : quemadmodum in Enchiridio Augustinus fatetur ; imo in omnibus reprobis relucet, et commendatur justitia tua atque potentia.
paras.en: But I think it better that nothing be understood: indeed, if we weigh it well, nothing will be seen to need supplying. For we ought to follow the Apostle's exposition. And the Apostle brings in and cites these words to the Romans in this way: [[Rom 3:4|God is true and every man a liar, as it is written: That thou mayest be justified in thy words and mayest overcome when thou art judged|Est autem Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax, sicut scriptum est, Ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis, et vincas quum judicaris]]. It is clear, then, that according to the Apostle's meaning holy David brought in these words in this sense: that God is justified by our iniquity, and overcomes when he is judged. And this is plainer still from the Apostle's next words, for he adds: [[Rom 3:5|if our injustice commend the justice of God, what shall we say?|Si autem iniquitas nostra justitiam Dei commendat, quid dicemus]] Yet it must be understood that God's being justified and glorified by our sin, and overcoming when he is judged, can be taken in two ways. First, causally and directly: and so it is not true. Secondly, occasionally and indirectly, or consequentially [that is, our sin is not the cause of God's being justified, but the occasion on which his justice appears]: and so it is true, as the Apostle brings it in. And this is the more literal sense, though the first exposition can stand. The sense, then, is: [[50:6|To thee only have I sinned, and have done evil before thee|Tibi soli peccavi et malum coram te feci]], so that from this, by occasion and in consequence, [[50:6|thou mayst be justified in thy words|justificeris in sermonibus tuis]], in which thou hast said through the Prophets that no man is without sin, but that every man is a liar[[Ps 115:2||]] [the margin gives Ps. cxv, 11, the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate it is Ps 115:2] in word or deed or some vice: because, as is written in the book of Job, No one is clean from filth[[Job 15:14||]][[Job 25:4||]] [the margin gives Job xv, 14 and xxv, 4, which say the like; Denis's words are the old Latin reading of Job 14:4]. Or, [[50:6|in thy words|In sermonibus tuis]], in which thou condemnest and punishest the sinner, but savest and glorifiest the just. For my evil, well ordered by thee, that is, justly punished or mercifully forgiven, turns to thy glory, as Augustine declares in the Enchiridion; nay, in all the reprobate thy justice and power shine out and are commended.

paras.t: Denique, ut plenius loquar, verba prædicta quadrupliciter exponi possunt. Jam enim duobus modis exposita sunt. Tertio autem exponuntur : Tibi soli peccavi et malum coram te feci, ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis, id est, quatenus consecutive seu concomitanter justus appareas in verbis quibus promisisti te incarnandum ex semine meo. Dum enim ego tam dire peccavi, et tu nihilo minus imples quod promisisti, patet quod non propter merita mea, sed propter tuam justitiam qua promissa adimples, humanam naturam ex stirpe mea assumas, et vincas alios in æquitate, quum judicaris a populo non te debere promissa implere propter enormitatem peccatorum meorum. — Quarto exponitur sic : Tibi soli peccavi et malum coram te feci, ut justificeris, id est, quatenus tu solus verus comproberis in sermonibus tuis, et vincas quum judicaris sic vel sic debuisse fecisse; vel, quum a Pilato atque Judæis judicaris ad mortem, qui sine dolo et culpa existis, et propter mea delicta omnia pateris : sicque per modum sequelæ ex meo peccato justificaris.
paras.en: Lastly, to speak more fully, these words can be expounded in four ways. Two ways have been given already. Thirdly, they are expounded thus: [[50:6|To thee only have I sinned, and have done evil before thee: that thou mayst be justified in thy words|Tibi soli peccavi et malum coram te feci, ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis]], that is, so that in consequence, or concomitantly, thou mayst appear just in the words in which thou didst promise to become incarnate of my seed. For since I have sinned so grievously, and thou nevertheless fulfillest what thou didst promise, it is clear that it is not for my merits but for thy justice, by which thou fulfillest thy promises, that thou takest human nature from my stock; [[50:6|and mayst overcome|et vincas]] others in equity, [[50:6|when thou art judged|quum judicaris]] by the people not to be bound to fulfil thy promises because of the enormity of my sins. — Fourthly it is expounded thus: [[50:6|To thee only have I sinned, and have done evil before thee: that thou mayst be justified|Tibi soli peccavi et malum coram te feci, ut justificeris]], that is, so that thou alone mayst be proved true [[50:6|in thy words|in sermonibus tuis]], [[50:6|and mayst overcome when thou art judged|et vincas quum judicaris]] to have been bound to act in this way or that; or, when thou art judged to death by Pilate and the Jews[[Matt 27:26||]], thou who art without guile and fault, and sufferest all things for my offences: and thus, by way of consequence, thou art justified by my sin.

paras.t: Deinde Propheta fragilitatem ac pronitatem mortalis naturæ ad culpam commemorat, quatenus per hoc Deum ad pietatem ac veniam provocet et inclinet, secundum quod Noe in Genesi ipse Deus spopondit : Nequaquam, inquiens, ultra maledicam terræ propter homines ; sensus enim et cogitatio cordis humani, proni sunt ad malum ab adolescentia sua. Ait ergo David : Ecce enim in iniquitatibus conceptus sum : tanquam dicat, Bene misereri te decet mihi fragili peccatori, quia ecce in vitiis conceptus sum, et in peccatis concepit me mater mea. Quoniam ergo fomes peccati mihi innatus est, mirum non est quod in peccatum prolapsus sum.
paras.en: Next the Prophet recalls the frailty of mortal nature and its proneness to sin, so as thereby to move and incline God to loving-kindness and pardon, as God himself promised Noe in Genesis: [[Gen 8:21|I will no more|Nequaquam]], he says, [[Gen 8:21|curse the earth for the sake of man: for the imagination and thought of man's heart are prone to evil from his youth|ultra maledicam terræ propter homines ; sensus enim et cogitatio cordis humani, proni sunt ad malum ab adolescentia sua]]. David says, then: [[50:7|For behold I was conceived in iniquities|Ecce enim in iniquitatibus conceptus sum]]: as though he said, It well becomes thee to have mercy on me, a frail sinner, for behold I was conceived in vices, [[50:7|and in sins did my mother conceive me|et in peccatis concepit me mater mea]]. Since, then, the tinder of sin [*fomes peccati*: the inclination to sin left in us by original sin] is inborn in me, it is no wonder that I have fallen into sin.

paras.t: Sed quomodo potest homo in iniquitatibus concipi, quum subjectum peccati et virtutis non sit nisi in anima seu intellectuali essentia, quæ corpori humano non statim in conceptione infunditur ? Iterum quæritur, quomodo in iniquitatibus concipiatur, quum non concipiatur nisi in originali peccato, quod non est nisi unum peccatum, sicut originalis justitia non erat nisi una virtus. Et respondendum, quod originale peccatum cum semine transfunditur ; non est tamen in semine ut in subjecto, sed ut in radice : et ergo anima mox quum semini sic infecto infunditur, maculatur et originali peccato coinquinatur. Cujus exemplum est de semine leprosi. Leprosus enim non nisi leprosum generat, et lepra cum semine transfunditur ; non est tamen in semine ut in subjecto, sed quasi in radice : anima vero infusa, statim proles contrahit lepram ex seminis infectione. Ad secundum dicendum, quod originale peccatum formaliter unum est, utpote carentia originalis justitiæ debitæ inesse ; materialiter vero est multa, propter quatuor animæ vulnera ex originali peccato secuta, quæ sunt, ignorantia, malitia, infirmitas et concupiscentia : sicut superius dictum est.
paras.en: But how can a man be conceived in iniquities, since the subject of sin and of virtue is only in the soul, or intellectual being, which is not poured into the human body at once at conception? Again it is asked how he is conceived in iniquities, since he is conceived only in original sin, which is but one sin, as original justice was but one virtue. The answer is that original sin is passed on with the seed; yet it is not in the seed as in its subject, but as in its root; and so the soul, as soon as it is poured into seed thus infected, is stained and defiled with original sin. An example of this is the seed of a leper. For a leper begets only a leper, and the leprosy is passed on with the seed; yet it is not in the seed as in its subject, but as it were in its root: but once the soul is infused, the offspring at once contracts leprosy from the infection of the seed. To the second it must be said that original sin is formally one, being the lack of the original justice that ought to be present; but materially it is many, because of the four wounds of the soul that followed from original sin, which are ignorance, malice, weakness and concupiscence: as was said above.

paras.t: Tertio quæri potest, quomodo parentes originale peccatum transfundant, quum tamen in Baptismo dimissum sit peccatum originale merito passionis dominicæ. Et respondendum, quod licet dimissum sit quantum ad reatum pœnæ seu maculam, non tamen fomes seu inclinatio omnino exstinguitur, quamvis debilitetur. Sed tunc fortius investigatur, quomodo peccatum istud transfundi in omnibus possit, quum tamen ipse concubitus maritalis omni possit peccato carere, imo et virtuosus ac meritorius esse, in quantum est actus justitiæ, qui ab Apostolo præcipitur, dicente, Uxori vir debitum reddat, et uxor viro (nullum autem peccatum, seu peccato inseparabiliter annexum, præcipitur) ; item in quantum est actus religionis ; tertio, in quantum est actus sacramenti. Et respondendum, quod parentes peccatum originale non transfundunt secundum quod particulares et proximæ causæ generationis exsistunt, vel quia in ipso concubitu semper seu inevitabiliter peccent, sed in quantum ex corrupta radice prodierunt. Per hoc quippe proles originale peccatum incurrit, unde ad originalem justitiam aliquo modo tenetur : non autem ad eam tenetur in quantum a primis parentibus nascitur, sed secundum quod a primis parentibus propagatur, tam secundum rationem seminalem, quam secundum corruptam substantiam.
paras.en: Thirdly, it may be asked how parents pass on original sin, when original sin has been forgiven them in Baptism by the merit of the Lord's passion. The answer is that although it has been forgiven as to the liability to punishment, or the stain, yet the tinder, or inclination, is not wholly put out, though it is weakened. But then the question presses harder, how this sin can be passed on in all, since the marriage act itself can be wholly without sin, nay can be virtuous and meritorious: in so far as it is an act of justice, which is commanded by the Apostle, who says, [[1 Cor 7:3|Let the husband render the debt to his wife: and the wife also in like manner to the husband|Uxori vir debitum reddat, et uxor viro]] (and no sin, nor anything inseparably bound up with sin, is commanded); again, in so far as it is an act of religion; and thirdly, in so far as it is the act of a sacrament. The answer is that parents do not pass on original sin as being the particular and proximate causes of generation, nor because they always or unavoidably sin in the act itself, but in so far as they have come from a corrupted root. For it is by this that the offspring incurs original sin, whereby it is in some way bound to original justice [that is, owes the original justice it lacks]: yet it is not bound to it in so far as it is born of the first parents, but in so far as it is propagated from the first parents [so the print, both times; in the first place the sense seems to require "born of its immediate parents"], both according to the seminal principle and according to the corrupted substance.

paras.t: Ecce enim veritatem dilexisti. Quasi dicat : Quia tu veritatem diligis, ego propriam culpam sine excusatione confiteor ; et quia ago quod complacet tibi, decet te mihi propitium fieri. Unde ait Salvator : Cognoscetis veritatem, et veritas liberabit vos. Deus autem veritatem potissimum diligit : nam similitudo est causa amoris. Quoniam ergo Deus naturaliter verus est, et essentialiter veritas increata, constat quod veritatem naturaliter diligit.
